description: Choice of OCR engine, acceptable error thresholds, and how errors are handled in the user flow.

threads.question: Is Tesseract OCR sufficient, or will you invest in fine-tuning / a paid OCR service?
threads.context: Receipt OCR is harder than document OCR — thermal paper, varied fonts, faded ink, curved scans.

posts.author: user
posts.message: Let's go with open source decent model, since we also want user to confirm before accepting the result.

posts.author: ai
posts.message:
Open source is fine for MVP. However, Tesseract is not the best open source option for receipts — it was designed for clean document text and struggles with thermal receipt fonts, low-contrast backgrounds, and mixed languages (important for Singapore where receipts may have English + Chinese or Malay characters).

Recommendation: use PaddleOCR instead of Tesseract.
- It's open source (Apache 2.0 licence), free to use commercially
- Significantly more accurate on receipts, especially multilingual (English + Chinese is natively supported)
- Has an active Python library (paddlepaddle + paddleocr)
- Works well with your existing plan of a Python microservice (see T20)
- Used in production by large companies, not just hobby projects

Pre-processing pipeline before OCR (regardless of engine):
1. Deskew (straighten tilted receipt)
2. Increase contrast (thermal paper is often low contrast)
3. Denoise
4. Scale to standard DPI

OpenCV handles all four in Python. Without preprocessing, even the best OCR engine will underperform on real-world receipt photos.

posts.author: user
posts.message: put a high level plan (under 50 words) to use PaddleOCR and preprocessing

posts.author: ai
posts.message: Plan: OpenCV preprocessing (deskew, contrast, denoise, scale) → PaddleOCR (English+Chinese model) → user confirmation loop. Good balance of accuracy and zero licensing cost for MVP.

threads.question: What is your acceptable OCR error rate for the retailer comparison to remain trustworthy?
threads.context: Errors in price data pushed to the shared comparison DB corrupt the comparison for all users.

posts.author: ai
posts.message:
20% error rate is acceptable for personal expense TRACKING — the user sees the OCR output, corrects it, and saves. Their own data is correct after confirmation.

However, 20% is too high for data that flows into the shared COMPARISON DATABASE. Here's why: if 1 in 5 price entries in the comparison pool is wrong, users will see comparison results that are occasionally misleading. For example: 'Sheng Siong has milk for $1.50' when the actual price is $2.50 — an OCR misread that was never corrected because it went straight to the pool. That erodes trust in the entire comparison feature.

Suggested two-tier error policy:

- PERSONAL TRACKING: 20% OCR error rate OK, user confirms and corrects
- COMPARISON DB CONTRIBUTION: Only user-CONFIRMED line items are ever submitted. The rule is simple — no unconfirmed data ever leaves the device/personal account for the shared pool. The user's confirmed version is what gets anonymised and submitted.

This means your comparison DB is always 0% unconfirmed data, regardless of OCR quality. The OCR accuracy matters for UX speed (fewer corrections = better experience), but data quality in the shared pool is protected by the confirmation gate.

posts.author: user
posts.message: so then should the confirmation gate be mandated ?

posts.author: ai
posts.message:
I’d argue yes, the confirmation gate should be mandatory for any line item submitted to the comparison DB. The trust in pricing data is the entire value prop of that feature — one bad apple spoils the bunch, and users will quickly stop relying on it if they see junk prices.

That said, we should make the confirmation step as frictionless as possible: auto-confirm items that look consistent (e.g., total matches sum of line items, no outliers vs previous receipts), and only surface ambiguous ones for review. This keeps the gate closed by default but doesn’t punish users with extra taps on clean data.

If we allowed an opt-out, the feature would degrade over time, and we’d be back to the original trust problem. So mandate it, but invest in smart defaults to minimise burden.

posts.author: ai
posts.message:
Glad we’re aligned. Let’s move forward by defining the heuristics for auto-confirmation. The key is to set clear rules: line items where the sum of prices matches the receipt total, prices fall within a reasonable range vs. historical data for that store, and no duplicate inconsistencies get automatically confirmed. We’ll also need a UI treatment that makes manual confirmation obvious but quick—maybe a single tap to accept a flagged item or a “confirm all shown” button for visually scanned receipts.

Once the logic is solid, we can prototype the flow and test with a subset of users to ensure the burden stays low. If the heuristics are tight enough, most items will auto-confirm and the comparison DB stays clean without much extra effort from anyone. Let’s sync on the exact rules before we start coding.

threads.question: How will you handle faded/poor quality receipt scans?
threads.context: Thermal paper fades over time; photos taken at odd angles or in low light are common.

posts.author: user
posts.message: If error rate is > 20%, we prompt user that image is not clear, retry or enter manually.

posts.author: ai
posts.message:
Good fallback. Two additions to make this smoother:

1. BEFORE the upload: do a quick image quality check on-device (blur detection using Laplacian variance is a simple, fast check). If the photo is clearly blurry, prompt immediately to retake before even sending to the backend — saves latency and server cost.

2. PARTIAL SUCCESS: instead of rejecting the entire receipt when quality is poor, surface the fields that were extracted with high confidence and let the user fill in just the gaps. A receipt with 8/10 items correctly read is more useful than a full manual re-entry prompt.
